IF f CONTAINS "\\start menu\\programs\\startup\\": ALERT Medium "Startup folder file: " + f
IF extension(f) IN EXEC_EXT AND writer IN (RISKY_PARENTS + INTERPRETERS):
ALERT High writer + " wrote executable content: " + f

events.name: Sysmon: Registry value set
events.description: Logged when a registry value is written. Focused on autostart locations, it catches one of the most common persistence methods.
how_to_enable: Install Sysmon with RegistryEvent rules for Run/RunOnce, Services, Winlogon, IFEO and similar autostart keys.

key_fields.why: Value data (often the command that will run).

attacks.name: Registry Run Key Persistence
attacks.summary: Adding a value under Run/RunOnce keys makes a program start every time a user logs on. It is simple, common, and easy to detect when monitored.
indicators: New values under ...\CurrentVersion\Run or RunOnce.
Values pointing to user-writable paths or script interpreters.
Writes by unusual processes (scripts, Office).
false_positives: Many legitimate apps add Run keys on install.

detect: Filter TargetObject to autostart keys (Run, RunOnce, Winlogon Shell/Userinit, IFEO Debugger).
Score Details for interpreters, encoded content, or user-writable paths.
Alert on high scores; log the rest for weekly review.
investigate: Inspect the referenced file.
Check which process wrote the key and how it started.
Build a timeline of what the same account and machine did 30 minutes before and after the event.
respond: Delete the value and the referenced file.
Preserve the relevant logs before making changes.
If the activity is malicious, open an incident and follow your response playbook.
prevent: Limit admin rights (HKLM keys need admin).
Application control.
Review at least quarterly who holds the rights involved in this event.

pseudocode: AUTOSTART = ["\\currentversion\\run", "\\currentversion\\runonce",
"\\winlogon\\shell", "\\winlogon\\userinit", "\\image file execution options\\"]
FOR EACH e IN Sysmon WHERE EventID == 13
IF lower(e.TargetObject) CONTAINS ANY AUTOSTART:
score = 0
IF references_user_writable_path(e.Details): score += 2
IF lower(e.Details) CONTAINS ANY INTERPRETERS: score += 2
IF basename(e.Image) IN (INTERPRETERS + RISKY_PARENTS): score += 1
IF score >= 2: ALERT Medium "Suspicious autostart entry: " + e.TargetObject

events.name: Sysmon: DNS query
events.description: Records DNS lookups along with the process that made them. It lets you tie suspicious domains directly to programs.
how_to_enable: Install Sysmon (v10+) with DnsQuery rules; exclude very common domains to reduce volume.

attacks.name: DNS-based C2 and Tunneling
attacks.summary: Malware can hide communications inside DNS queries, or generate many random domain names (DGA) to find its server. Both create unusual DNS patterns.
indicators: Very long or high-entropy subdomains.
Large numbers of unique subdomains of one parent domain from one host.
Many NXDOMAIN-style lookups of random names.
false_positives: CDNs and some security products use long generated names.

detect: Compute length and entropy of the left-most labels of QueryName.
Count unique subdomains per parent domain per host per hour.
Weight by rarity of the parent domain across the environment.
Allow-list known CDNs and security vendors.
investigate: Identify the process and inspect it.
Look up the parent domain's registration age.
Build a timeline of what the same account and machine did 30 minutes before and after the event.
respond: Sinkhole or block the domain.
Isolate the host.
Preserve the relevant logs before making changes.
prevent: Force all DNS through internal resolvers with filtering.
Block direct outbound DNS (port 53) from endpoints.
Review at least quarterly who holds the rights involved in this event.

pseudocode: FOR EACH (host, parent) IN GROUP Sysmon WHERE EventID == 22 BY Computer, registered_domain(QueryName) OVER 1 hour
IF parent IN dns_allow_list: CONTINUE
subs = DISTINCT subdomain(QueryName)
avg_entropy = MEAN(entropy(s) FOR s IN subs); avg_len = MEAN(length(s) FOR s IN subs)
IF COUNT(subs) >= 50 AND (avg_entropy > 3.8 OR avg_len > 40):
ALERT High "Possible DNS tunneling to " + parent + " from " + host

events.name: The event logging service has shut down
events.description: The Windows Event Log service stopped. This is normal during a shutdown, but on a running system it means no further events will be recorded until the service restarts.
how_to_enable: This event is always recorded by Windows; no audit policy setting is needed.
Forward the Security log to your SIEM so the event is kept even if the local log is cleared or overwritten.
events.attack_context: Attackers who want to hide their activity may try to stop, fill up or disrupt the event log so their actions are never recorded. An unexpected log shutdown, dropped events or a full log can be a sign that someone is trying to blind defenders.
mitre: T1562.002 Impair Defenses: Disable Windows Event Logging
T1070.001 Indicator Removal: Clear Windows Event Logs

key_fields.why: When it happened; compare with surrounding activity.

watch_for: Occurrences outside planned maintenance or reboots.
The same event on several machines within a short time.
Gaps in the log right after this event (the host went quiet).
Nearby events such as 1102 (log cleared) or 4719 (audit policy changed).

attacks.name: Logging disruption
attacks.summary: Attackers who want to hide their activity may try to stop, fill up or disrupt the event log so their actions are never recorded. An unexpected log shutdown, dropped events or a full log can be a sign that someone is trying to blind defenders.
indicators: Occurrences outside planned maintenance or reboots.
The same event on several machines within a short time.
Gaps in the log right after this event (the host went quiet).
Nearby events such as 1102 (log cleared) or 4719 (audit policy changed).
false_positives: Log size misconfiguration on busy servers.

detect: Forward the Security log in near real time so events survive a local problem.
Alert on event 1100 from servers and domain controllers.
Ignore occurrences that line up with an approved reboot or maintenance window.
Raise severity if the same event appears on several machines within an hour.
investigate: Check whether the machine rebooted (4608/4609) or the service was stopped by a user.
Look for a gap in the machine's events after this time.
Review process activity (4688) just before the event.
respond: Restore logging and confirm events are flowing again.
If a person or program caused it, contain the machine and investigate that account.
Preserve the relevant logs before making changes.
prevent: Set an adequate log size and 'overwrite as needed' or archive policy.
Forward logs centrally and alert when a machine stops sending events.
Review at least quarterly who holds the rights involved in this event.

pseudocode: FOR EACH event IN Security WHERE EventID == 1100
IF in_maintenance_window(event.Computer, event.Time): CONTINUE
hosts = DISTINCT Computer WITH EventID == 1100 IN 60 minutes
sev = IF COUNT(hosts) >= 3 THEN "High" ELSE "Medium"
ALERT sev "Logging disruption (1100) on " + event.Computer

events.name: Audit events have been dropped by the transport
events.description: Windows could not deliver some audit events to the log, so part of the audit trail is missing. It usually points to overload or a logging problem.
how_to_enable: This event is always recorded by Windows; no audit policy setting is needed.

attacks.name: Logging disruption
attacks.summary: Attackers who want to hide their activity may try to stop, fill up or disrupt the event log so their actions are never recorded. An unexpected log shutdown, dropped events or a full log can be a sign that someone is trying to blind defenders.
indicators: Occurrences outside planned maintenance or reboots.
The same event on several machines within a short time.
Gaps in the log right after this event (the host went quiet).
Nearby events such as 1102 (log cleared) or 4719 (audit policy changed).
false_positives: Log size misconfiguration on busy servers.

detect: Forward the Security log in near real time so events survive a local problem.
Alert on event 1105 from servers and domain controllers.
Ignore occurrences that line up with an approved reboot or maintenance window.
Raise severity if the same event appears on several machines within an hour.
investigate: Check whether the machine rebooted (4608/4609) or the service was stopped by a user.
Look for a gap in the machine's events after this time.
Review process activity (4688) just before the event.
respond: Restore logging and confirm events are flowing again.
If a person or program caused it, contain the machine and investigate that account.
Preserve the relevant logs before making changes.
prevent: Set an adequate log size and 'overwrite as needed' or archive policy.
Forward logs centrally and alert when a machine stops sending events.
Review at least quarterly who holds the rights involved in this event.

pseudocode: FOR EACH event IN Security WHERE EventID == 1105
IF in_maintenance_window(event.Computer, event.Time): CONTINUE
hosts = DISTINCT Computer WITH EventID == 1105 IN 60 minutes
sev = IF COUNT(hosts) >= 3 THEN "High" ELSE "Medium"
ALERT sev "Logging disruption (1105) on " + event.Computer

events.name: Windows is starting up
events.description: Windows started up. Every boot records this event, which is useful for building a timeline.
how_to_enable: Open Group Policy Management and edit a GPO linked to the computers you want to monitor.
Go to Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Advanced Audit Policy Configuration > System.
Enable 'Audit Security State Change' for Success and/or Failure as needed.
Run 'gpupdate /force' on a test machine and confirm with 'auditpol /get /subcategory:"Security State Change"'.
Forward the Security log to your SIEM (Windows Event Forwarding or an agent).
events.attack_context: Startups, shutdowns and clock changes give defenders context. Attackers may reboot a machine to load something they installed, or change the system time to confuse the order of events and break time-based authentication such as Kerberos.

key_fields.why: When it happened; compare with surrounding activity.

watch_for: Reboots of servers outside maintenance windows.
Time changes by users (rather than the Windows time service) or large jumps in time.
Recovery from CrashOnAuditFail, which means auditing had stopped the system.

attacks.name: Unexpected system state change
attacks.summary: Startups, shutdowns and clock changes give defenders context. Attackers may reboot a machine to load something they installed, or change the system time to confuse the order of events and break time-based authentication such as Kerberos.
indicators: Reboots of servers outside maintenance windows.
Time changes by users (rather than the Windows time service) or large jumps in time.
Recovery from CrashOnAuditFail, which means auditing had stopped the system.
false_positives: Normal time synchronisation by the Windows Time service.

detect: Collect event 4608 from servers and domain controllers.
For time changes (4616), ignore changes made by the time service (svchost / LOCAL SERVICE).
For reboots and shutdowns, compare against approved maintenance windows.
Alert on the remaining events, especially on domain controllers.
investigate: Identify who or what caused the change (SubjectUserName, process).
Check logons and process activity shortly before the event.
For clock changes, check whether timestamps around the event look out of order.
respond: Correct the clock or restore service as needed.
Investigate the account involved if the change was not planned.
Preserve the relevant logs before making changes.
prevent: Restrict the 'Change the system time' and 'Shut down the system' rights on servers.
Use a reliable time source for all domain members.
Review at least quarterly who holds the rights involved in this event.

ALERT Medium "Unexpected system state change (4608) on " + event.Computer

events.name: An authentication package has been loaded by the Local Security Authority
events.description: An authentication package was loaded by LSA at startup. Standard ones include msv1_0; anything unfamiliar deserves review.
how_to_enable: Open Group Policy Management and edit a GPO linked to the computers you want to monitor.
Go to Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Advanced Audit Policy Configuration > System.
Enable 'Audit Security System Extension' for Success and/or Failure as needed.
Run 'gpupdate /force' on a test machine and confirm with 'auditpol /get /subcategory:"Security System Extension"'.
Forward the Security log to your SIEM (Windows Event Forwarding or an agent).
events.attack_context: The Local Security Authority (LSA) handles logons and passwords. Attackers who already have admin rights may try to make LSA load an extra package or DLL so they can capture credentials or keep access after a reboot. New or unfamiliar packages are therefore worth a close look.

key_fields.why: When it happened; compare with surrounding activity.
Name and path of what was loaded; compare with a known-good baseline.

watch_for: Package names that are not on your baseline of standard Windows packages.
DLL paths outside C:\Windows\System32.
New packages appearing after a recent admin logon or software install you cannot explain.

attacks.name: Suspicious LSA / authentication package
attacks.summary: The Local Security Authority (LSA) handles logons and passwords. Attackers who already have admin rights may try to make LSA load an extra package or DLL so they can capture credentials or keep access after a reboot. New or unfamiliar packages are therefore worth a close look.
indicators: Package names that are not on your baseline of standard Windows packages.
DLL paths outside C:\Windows\System32.
New packages appearing after a recent admin logon or software install you cannot explain.
false_positives: New security software or smart-card middleware.

detect: Build a baseline of package names reported by event 4610 on a clean machine of each build.
Alert when a package name is not in the baseline.
Alert when a package loads from outside C:\Windows\System32.
Review the baseline after every Windows feature update.
investigate: Find the DLL on disk, check its signature and hash.
Check registry locations that list LSA packages for recent changes.
Identify when and by whom it was installed (4688, 4657).
respond: Isolate the machine.
Remove the unauthorized package and reboot.
Reset passwords for accounts that logged on while it was loaded.
prevent: Enable LSA protection (RunAsPPL) so only signed packages can load.
Limit local administrator rights.
Review at least quarterly who holds the rights involved in this event.

pseudocode: FOR EACH event IN Security WHERE EventID == 4610
pkg = lower(event.PackageName)
IF pkg NOT IN lsa_package_baseline[os_build(event.Computer)]:
ALERT High "Unknown LSA package loaded: " + pkg
ELSE IF NOT path_in(pkg_path(pkg), "C:\\Windows\\System32"):
ALERT High "LSA package loaded from unusual path"

events.name: Internal resources allocated for the queuing of audit messages have been exhausted, leading to the loss of some audits
events.description: Windows ran out of resources for queuing audit messages, so some events were lost. It can happen under heavy load or deliberate flooding.
how_to_enable: Open Group Policy Management and edit a GPO linked to the computers you want to monitor.
Go to Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Advanced Audit Policy Configuration > System.
Enable 'Audit System Integrity' for Success and/or Failure as needed.
Run 'gpupdate /force' on a test machine and confirm with 'auditpol /get /subcategory:"System Integrity"'.
Forward the Security log to your SIEM (Windows Event Forwarding or an agent).
events.attack_context: These events report problems with Windows' own security checks: invalid file signatures, tampering with protected processes, or audit messages being lost. Attackers who modify system files or try to load unsigned code can trigger them.

key_fields.why: When it happened; compare with surrounding activity.
Which file or process failed the check.

watch_for: Code integrity failures for files in system folders.
Repeated failures for the same file across machines (possible tampered software).
Integrity or crypto self-test failures on servers.

attacks.name: System integrity violation
attacks.summary: These events report problems with Windows' own security checks: invalid file signatures, tampering with protected processes, or audit messages being lost. Attackers who modify system files or try to load unsigned code can trigger them.
indicators: Code integrity failures for files in system folders.
Repeated failures for the same file across machines (possible tampered software).
Integrity or crypto self-test failures on servers.

detect: Collect event 4612 from all machines.
Alert on integrity failures for files in Windows system folders.
Count how many machines report the same file; one file on many machines suggests a tampered package.
Treat any occurrence on a domain controller as high priority.
investigate: Get the file path and hash, and compare it with a known-good copy.
Check recent software installs or updates on the machine.
Look for other signs of tampering (new services 7045, driver loads).
respond: Replace the file from a trusted source or reimage the machine.
Isolate the machine if tampering is suspected.
Preserve the relevant logs before making changes.
prevent: Enable Windows Defender Application Control and HVCI.
Keep systems patched and restrict administrator rights.
Review at least quarterly who holds the rights involved in this event.

pseudocode: FOR EACH event IN Security WHERE EventID == 4612
f = lower(event.FileName)
spread = COUNT DISTINCT Computer WITH EventID == 4612 AND FileName == f IN 24 hours
sev = "Medium"
IF path_in(f, "c:\\windows\\") OR is_domain_controller(event.Computer): sev = "High"
ALERT sev "Integrity violation (4612) for " + f + " on " + spread + " host(s)"

events.name: Boot Configuration Data loaded
events.description: Windows loaded its Boot Configuration Data at startup. The event lists key boot security settings, so it is a quick way to check they are as expected.
how_to_enable: Open Group Policy Management and edit a GPO linked to the computers you want to monitor.
Go to Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Advanced Audit Policy Configuration > Policy Change.
Enable 'Audit Other Policy Change Events' for Success and/or Failure as needed.
Run 'gpupdate /force' on a test machine and confirm with 'auditpol /get /subcategory:"Other Policy Change Events"'.
Forward the Security log to your SIEM (Windows Event Forwarding or an agent).
events.attack_context: Boot configuration controls how Windows starts, including security features like Secure Boot checks and test signing. Attackers may change it to weaken protections before the operating system loads.

key_fields.why: When it happened; compare with surrounding activity.
Security-relevant boot options that were loaded.

watch_for: Test signing or kernel debugging enabled on production machines.
Security features such as virtualization-based security reported as disabled.

attacks.name: Weakened boot security settings
attacks.summary: Boot configuration controls how Windows starts, including security features like Secure Boot checks and test signing. Attackers may change it to weaken protections before the operating system loads.
indicators: Test signing or kernel debugging enabled on production machines.
Security features such as virtualization-based security reported as disabled.
false_positives: Developer or lab machines with test signing enabled on purpose.

detect: Collect event 4826 at every boot.
Parse the boot security fields (test signing, kernel debugging, virtualization-based security).
Alert when a production machine boots with test signing or kernel debugging enabled.
Alert when security features are reported off where your standard says on.
investigate: Check who changed the boot configuration and when (4688 for bcdedit).
Look for unsigned drivers loaded after the reboot.
Build a timeline of what the same account and machine did 30 minutes before and after the event.
respond: Restore the standard boot configuration and reboot.
Investigate the machine for rootkits or unsigned drivers.
Preserve the relevant logs before making changes.
prevent: Enable Secure Boot and BitLocker with TPM.
Restrict administrator access to production machines.
Review at least quarterly who holds the rights involved in this event.

pseudocode: FOR EACH event IN Security WHERE EventID == 4826
IF is_production(event.Computer)
AND (event.TestSigning == "Yes" OR event.KernelDebug == "Yes"):
ALERT High "Weakened boot settings on " + event.Computer

events.name: An account was logged off
events.description: A logon session ended. Windows records it when the session is destroyed, sometimes a little after the user actually left.
how_to_enable: Open Group Policy Management and edit a GPO linked to the computers you want to monitor.
Go to Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Advanced Audit Policy Configuration > Logon/Logoff.
Enable 'Audit Logoff' for Success and/or Failure as needed.
Run 'gpupdate /force' on a test machine and confirm with 'auditpol /get /subcategory:"Logoff"'.
Forward the Security log to your SIEM (Windows Event Forwarding or an agent).
events.attack_context: Logoff events do not reveal attacks by themselves, but they close the timeline. Pairing each logon with its logoff shows how long an attacker's session lasted and what happened in between.

key_fields.why: Links this event to the matching 4624 logon for the same session.
The machine where the session exists.
Same meaning as in 4624 (3 = network, 10 = RDP, etc.).

watch_for: Very short sessions by privileged accounts on many hosts (quick in-and-out activity).
Sessions for suspicious logons: use TargetLogonId to find when they ended.

attacks.name: Session timeline (logon to logoff)
attacks.summary: Logoff events do not reveal attacks by themselves, but they close the timeline. Pairing each logon with its logoff shows how long an attacker's session lasted and what happened in between.
indicators: Very short sessions by privileged accounts on many hosts (quick in-and-out activity).
Sessions for suspicious logons: use TargetLogonId to find when they ended.
false_positives: Service and batch sessions that start and end frequently.

detect: Collect event 4634 along with 4624.
Join each logoff to its logon using TargetLogonId.
Calculate session duration per account and machine.
Flag privileged accounts with many very short sessions across many machines.
investigate: For a suspicious logon, find its logoff to bound the timeline.
Review everything that happened on the machine between logon and logoff.
Build a timeline of what the same account and machine did 30 minutes before and after the event.
respond: Use the session boundaries to scope what the account could have done.
Preserve the relevant logs before making changes.
If the activity is malicious, open an incident and follow your response playbook.
prevent: Limit where privileged accounts can log on.
Set idle session time limits for RDP.
Review at least quarterly who holds the rights involved in this event.

pseudocode: FOR EACH lo IN Security WHERE EventID == 4634
li = FIND 4624 WHERE TargetLogonId == lo.TargetLogonId AND Computer == lo.Computer
IF li IS NONE: CONTINUE
dur = lo.Time - li.Time
IF lo.TargetUserName IN privileged_accounts AND dur < 2 minutes:
short = COUNT such sessions FOR lo.TargetUserName IN 1 hour
IF short >= 5: ALERT Medium "Many short admin sessions: " + lo.TargetUserName

events.name: A replay attack was detected
events.description: Windows detected a replay attack: an authentication request that was a copy of an earlier one. It can indicate someone replaying captured traffic, or occasionally a misconfiguration.
how_to_enable: Open Group Policy Management and edit a GPO linked to the computers you want to monitor.
Go to Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Advanced Audit Policy Configuration > Logon/Logoff.
Enable 'Audit Other Logon/Logoff Events' for Success and/or Failure as needed.
Run 'gpupdate /force' on a test machine and confirm with 'auditpol /get /subcategory:"Other Logon/Logoff Events"'.
Forward the Security log to your SIEM (Windows Event Forwarding or an agent).
events.attack_context: A replay attack means someone sent a copy of an earlier authentication message, hoping to be accepted as the original user. Windows detected and blocked it, but the source deserves investigation.

key_fields.why: Links this event to the matching 4624 logon for the same session.
The machine where the session exists.
Where a reconnecting RDP session came from.

watch_for: The source machine of the replay.
Repeated replay detections, which suggest deliberate attempts.

attacks.name: Unusual interactive or remote session activity
attacks.summary: A replay attack means someone sent a copy of an earlier authentication message, hoping to be accepted as the original user. Windows detected and blocked it, but the source deserves investigation.
indicators: The source machine of the replay.
Repeated replay detections, which suggest deliberate attempts.

detect: Collect event 4649 from workstations and servers.
Build a baseline of normal hours and client machines for each user.
Flag events from new client names or addresses, or at unusual hours.
Increase severity for privileged accounts and servers.
investigate: Confirm with the user whether they were working at that time.
Match the event to the logon (4624) and review processes started in the session.
Build a timeline of what the same account and machine did 30 minutes before and after the event.
respond: Disconnect the session and reset credentials if unauthorized.
Contain the source machine.
Preserve the relevant logs before making changes.
prevent: Require MFA for remote access.
Limit RDP to jump hosts and approved users.
Review at least quarterly who holds the rights involved in this event.

pseudocode: FOR EACH event IN Security WHERE EventID == 4649
u = event.TargetUserName; client = COALESCE(event.ClientName, event.IpAddress)
score = 0
IF client NOT IN usual_clients[u]: score += 2

events.name: A Kerberos service ticket was renewed
events.description: A Kerberos service ticket was renewed. Normally routine; unusual only in volume or timing.
how_to_enable: Open Group Policy Management and edit a GPO linked to the computers you want to monitor.

events.attack_context: Service tickets let users reach services such as file shares and databases. Attackers request tickets to reach services, and sometimes to collect encrypted data they can attack offline. Failures and unusual renewals help reveal this.

key_fields.why: Account the ticket or request is for.
Why it failed; explains most Kerberos problems.
Weak types such as RC4 (0x17) deserve attention.
Which service the ticket is for.

watch_for: Bursts of failures from one client across many services.
Requests for services that no longer exist or rarely get used.
Tickets renewed far beyond normal working patterns.

attacks.name: Abnormal service ticket activity
attacks.summary: Service tickets let users reach services such as file shares and databases. Attackers request tickets to reach services, and sometimes to collect encrypted data they can attack offline. Failures and unusual renewals help reveal this.
indicators: Bursts of failures from one client across many services.
Requests for services that no longer exist or rarely get used.
Tickets renewed far beyond normal working patterns.
false_positives: Misconfigured applications pointing at retired services.

detect: Collect event 4770 from all domain controllers.
Group by client IP and account over one hour.
Alert when failures or requests span many different services compared with the normal baseline.
investigate: Identify the client machine and the process making requests.
Check for related 4769 RC4 requests.
Build a timeline of what the same account and machine did 30 minutes before and after the event.
respond: Contain the client machine if the activity is not explained.
Reset passwords of targeted service accounts if tickets may have been collected.
Preserve the relevant logs before making changes.
prevent: Use managed service accounts with long random passwords.
Disable RC4 where possible.
Review at least quarterly who holds the rights involved in this event.

ALERT Medium "Unusual Kerberos service ticket activity from " + ip

attacks.name: Saved credential access

detect: Collect event 5376 from workstations (volume can be high; filter where possible).
Count credential reads per user and process per hour.

Review at least quarterly who holds the rights involved in this event.

detect: Collect event 4741 from domain controllers.
Alert when the actor is an ordinary user rather than your deployment accounts.

Flag computer names that do not follow your naming standard.

attacks.summary: Security groups control access. Attackers create groups, change them, or quietly remove other members (including defenders) to gain control, hide access, or lock others out. Changes to privileged groups deserve immediate attention.
indicators: Any change to privileged groups (Domain Admins, Enterprise Admins, Administrators, Backup Operators...).
Changes made outside change windows or by unexpected accounts.
Group scope/type changes that turn a harmless group into a security group.

investigate: Confirm the change against an access request.

Review what the affected accounts did afterwards.
respond: Reverse the change.
Reset credentials of the actor if the change was unauthorized.
Preserve the relevant logs before making changes.
prevent: Keep sensitive groups small and use just-in-time access.

Review at least quarterly who holds the rights involved in this event.

events.name: A security-enabled local group membership was enumerated
events.description: The members of a security-enabled local group were listed. Enumerating the local Administrators group is common reconnaissance; look at the calling process.
how_to_enable: Open Group Policy Management and edit a GPO linked to the computers you want to monitor.
Go to Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Advanced Audit Policy Configuration > Account Management.
Enable 'Audit Security Group Management' for Success and/or Failure as needed.

events.attack_context: Before attackers act, they look around: which accounts exist, who is an administrator, which groups have access to what. Listing group memberships is a normal admin task, but a burst of these lookups from an unusual program or account is a classic sign of reconnaissance after a machine has been compromised.
mitre: T1069.001 Permission Groups Discovery: Local Groups

key_fields.why: Program that performed the lookup; the most useful field here.
User or group that was looked up.

watch_for: Many enumeration events from one account or process in a short time.
Lookups made by scripting tools or programs that do not normally query groups.
Enumeration shortly after a suspicious logon or a new process on the machine.
The CallerProcessName field: compare it with known admin and management tools.

detect: Collect event 4744 from domain controllers.

investigate: Check whether the group was later converted or used to grant access.

respond: Reverse unauthorized membership changes.

prevent: Limit who can manage groups that receive sensitive email.
Review at least quarterly who holds the rights involved in this event.

Privileged operations by accounts that are not administrators.

attacks.name: Sensitive privilege used by unusual process
attacks.summary: Blocked TPM commands are usually harmless application behavior, but repeated attempts could indicate software probing the TPM for functions it should not use.
indicators: SeDebugPrivilege, SeTcbPrivilege, SeLoadDriverPrivilege or SeTakeOwnershipPrivilege used by unfamiliar programs.
Privileged operations by accounts that are not administrators.

detect: Collect event 4671 (volume can be high; filter to the most sensitive privileges).
Focus on SeDebugPrivilege, SeTcbPrivilege, SeLoadDriverPrivilege, SeTakeOwnershipPrivilege.
Alert when these are used by processes not on your baseline.
investigate: Identify the process, its parent and hash.
Check for credential access (Sysmon 10) on the same machine.
Build a timeline of what the same account and machine did 30 minutes before and after the event.
respond: Isolate the machine and terminate the process if malicious.
Preserve the relevant logs before making changes.
If the activity is malicious, open an incident and follow your response playbook.
prevent: Remove sensitive user rights from accounts that do not need them.
Review at least quarterly who holds the rights involved in this event.
After every incident, feed the lessons learned back into this detection.

pseudocode: WATCH = ["SeDebugPrivilege", "SeTcbPrivilege", "SeLoadDriverPrivilege", "SeTakeOwnershipPrivilege"]
FOR EACH event IN Security WHERE EventID == 4671
IF event.PrivilegeList INTERSECTS WATCH AND basename(event.ProcessName) NOT IN privilege_baseline:
ALERT High "Sensitive privilege used by " + event.ProcessName

events.name: A process has exited
events.description: A process exited. Pair it with the 4688 that started it to know how long it ran.
how_to_enable: Open Group Policy Management and edit a GPO linked to the computers you want to monitor.
Go to Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Advanced Audit Policy Configuration > Detailed Tracking.
Enable 'Audit Process Termination' for Success and/or Failure as needed.
Run 'gpupdate /force' on a test machine and confirm with 'auditpol /get /subcategory:"Process Termination"'.
Forward the Security log to your SIEM (Windows Event Forwarding or an agent).
events.attack_context: Process exit events complete the process timeline. Very short-lived processes, or security tools that exit unexpectedly, can reveal an attacker running quick commands or stopping defenses.
mitre: T1562.001 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Tools

key_fields.why: Which process exited; match to its 4688.

watch_for: Security or monitoring tools exiting outside updates or reboots.

attacks.name: Security tool stopped
attacks.summary: Process exit events complete the process timeline. Very short-lived processes, or security tools that exit unexpectedly, can reveal an attacker running quick commands or stopping defenses.
indicators: Security or monitoring tools exiting outside updates or reboots.
false_positives: Updates and reboots of security software.

detect: Collect event 4689 from all machines.
Keep a list of security and monitoring process names.
Alert when one of them exits and no update or reboot explains it.
investigate: Check which account and process caused the exit (4688 before it).
Check whether the tool restarted.
Build a timeline of what the same account and machine did 30 minutes before and after the event.
respond: Restart the tool and isolate the machine if tampering is suspected.
Preserve the relevant logs before making changes.
If the activity is malicious, open an incident and follow your response playbook.
prevent: Enable tamper protection in your security software.
Review at least quarterly who holds the rights involved in this event.
After every incident, feed the lessons learned back into this detection.

pseudocode: FOR EACH event IN Security WHERE EventID == 4689

AND NOT update_or_reboot_near(event.Computer, event.Time):

events.name: Backup of data protection master key was attempted
events.description: Windows tried to back up a DPAPI master key (normally when the user changes their password).
how_to_enable: Open Group Policy Management and edit a GPO linked to the computers you want to monitor.
Go to Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Advanced Audit Policy Configuration > Detailed Tracking.
Enable 'Audit DPAPI Activity' for Success and/or Failure as needed.
Run 'gpupdate /force' on a test machine and confirm with 'auditpol /get /subcategory:"DPAPI Activity"'.
Forward the Security log to your SIEM (Windows Event Forwarding or an agent).
events.attack_context: DPAPI protects saved browser passwords, Wi-Fi keys and other secrets. Attackers who gain access may try to unprotect this data or retrieve DPAPI master keys (including the domain backup key) to decrypt secrets for many users.

key_fields.why: Account whose data or key was involved.
Which DPAPI master key and server were used.

watch_for: Master key recovery or backup activity that does not match normal password changes.
Large numbers of unprotect operations by unusual processes.

attacks.name: Unusual DPAPI activity
attacks.summary: DPAPI protects saved browser passwords, Wi-Fi keys and other secrets. Attackers who gain access may try to unprotect this data or retrieve DPAPI master keys (including the domain backup key) to decrypt secrets for many users.
indicators: Master key recovery or backup activity that does not match normal password changes.
Large numbers of unprotect operations by unusual processes.
false_positives: Normal decryption by browsers and apps.

detect: Collect event 4692 from workstations and domain controllers.
Alert on master key recovery that does not follow a password reset.
Alert on bursts of unprotect operations by unfamiliar processes.
investigate: Identify the process and user.
Check whether browser or saved credentials were then used elsewhere.
Build a timeline of what the same account and machine did 30 minutes before and after the event.
respond: Reset affected user passwords and revoke sessions.
Isolate the machine if malicious.
Preserve the relevant logs before making changes.
prevent: Enable Credential Guard.
Protect domain controllers, which hold the DPAPI domain backup key.
Review at least quarterly who holds the rights involved in this event.

pseudocode: FOR EACH event IN Security WHERE EventID == 4692
IF event.EventID == 4693 AND NOT EXISTS 4724 FOR event.SubjectUserName WITHIN 1 hour BEFORE:
ALERT Medium "DPAPI master key recovery without password reset"
FOR EACH (user, proc) IN GROUP Security WHERE EventID == 4692 BY SubjectUserName, ProcessName OVER 10 minutes
IF COUNT(events) > 5 * baseline(user, proc): ALERT Medium "DPAPI burst by " + proc

events.name: A scheduled task was deleted
events.description: A scheduled task was deleted. Deleting a task right after it ran can be an attempt to remove evidence.
how_to_enable: Open Group Policy Management and edit a GPO linked to the computers you want to monitor.
Go to Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Advanced Audit Policy Configuration > Object Access.
Enable 'Audit Other Object Access Events' for Success and/or Failure as needed.
Run 'gpupdate /force' on a test machine and confirm with 'auditpol /get /subcategory:"Other Object Access Events"'.
Forward the Security log to your SIEM (Windows Event Forwarding or an agent).
events.attack_context: Scheduled tasks can run programs automatically, often with high privileges. Attackers create or change tasks to keep access or run code, and delete them afterwards to clean up. Enabling or disabling tasks can also switch security jobs off.

key_fields.why: Name and folder of the task.
The task's full definition, including the command it runs.

watch_for: Tasks created, changed or deleted shortly after a remote logon.
Tasks that run scripts or programs from user-writable folders.
Security or backup tasks being disabled or deleted.

attacks.name: Scheduled task tampering
attacks.summary: Scheduled tasks can run programs automatically, often with high privileges. Attackers create or change tasks to keep access or run code, and delete them afterwards to clean up. Enabling or disabling tasks can also switch security jobs off.
indicators: Tasks created, changed or deleted shortly after a remote logon.
Tasks that run scripts or programs from user-writable folders.
Security or backup tasks being disabled or deleted.

detect: Collect event 4699 from all machines.
For updates, compare the new command with the previous version of the task.
Alert when a task runs scripts or programs from user-writable folders.
Alert when security or backup tasks are disabled or deleted.
investigate: Export the task definition and the file it runs.
Identify the actor's logon session and source.
Build a timeline of what the same account and machine did 30 minutes before and after the event.
respond: Restore or remove the task.
Hunt for the same task on other machines.
Preserve the relevant logs before making changes.
prevent: Limit administrator rights.
Use application control.
Review at least quarterly who holds the rights involved in this event.

pseudocode: FOR EACH event IN Security WHERE EventID == 4699
cmd = lower(task_command(event.TaskContent))
IF references_user_writable_path(cmd) OR cmd CONTAINS ANY INTERPRETERS:
ALERT High "A scheduled task was deleted: " + event.TaskName
ELSE IF event.TaskName IN security_tasks:
ALERT High "Security task changed: " + event.TaskName

events.attack_context: COM+ catalog changes register or alter components that other applications load. Attackers can abuse COM registrations so their code runs inside trusted programs.

What kind of access (read, write, delete...).

attacks.name: COM+ catalog change
attacks.summary: COM+ catalog changes register or alter components that other applications load. Attackers can abuse COM registrations so their code runs inside trusted programs.
indicators: COM+ changes on servers outside software installs.

detect: Collect event 5888 from servers.
Ignore changes during approved software installs.
Alert on other changes, especially by scripts or unusual accounts.
investigate: Identify the component that was changed and the files it points to.
Build a timeline of what the same account and machine did 30 minutes before and after the event.
Check whether the account or machine also appears in other alerts.
respond: Revert the COM+ change and remove unknown components.
Preserve the relevant logs before making changes.
If the activity is malicious, open an incident and follow your response playbook.
prevent: Restrict administrator rights on servers.
Review at least quarterly who holds the rights involved in this event.
After every incident, feed the lessons learned back into this detection.

IF NOT software_install_near(event.Computer, event.Time):
ALERT Medium "An object in the COM+ Catalog was modified on " + event.Computer

events.attack_context: COM+ catalog changes register or alter components that other applications load. Attackers can abuse COM registrations so their code runs inside trusted programs.
mitre: T1546.015 Event Triggered Execution: Component Object Model Hijacking

key_fields.why: The file, folder, registry key or object involved.
What kind of access (read, write, delete...).

watch_for: COM+ changes on servers outside software installs.

attacks.name: COM+ catalog change
attacks.summary: COM+ catalog changes register or alter components that other applications load. Attackers can abuse COM registrations so their code runs inside trusted programs.
indicators: COM+ changes on servers outside software installs.

detect: Collect event 5889 from servers.
Ignore changes during approved software installs.
Alert on other changes, especially by scripts or unusual accounts.
investigate: Identify the component that was changed and the files it points to.
Build a timeline of what the same account and machine did 30 minutes before and after the event.
Check whether the account or machine also appears in other alerts.
respond: Revert the COM+ change and remove unknown components.
Preserve the relevant logs before making changes.
If the activity is malicious, open an incident and follow your response playbook.
prevent: Restrict administrator rights on servers.
Review at least quarterly who holds the rights involved in this event.
After every incident, feed the lessons learned back into this detection.

events.attack_context: Attackers create or change network shares to stage stolen data, spread tools to other machines, or give themselves easy access. Removing shares can also disrupt the business.
mitre: T1021.002 Remote Services: SMB/Windows Admin Shares

key_fields.why: Which share and which folder it exposes.

watch_for: New shares on workstations (they rarely need any).
Share permissions changed to Everyone / Full Control.
Shares pointing at sensitive folders or the root of a drive.

attacks.name: Suspicious network share change
attacks.summary: Attackers create or change network shares to stage stolen data, spread tools to other machines, or give themselves easy access. Removing shares can also disrupt the business.
indicators: New shares on workstations (they rarely need any).
Share permissions changed to Everyone / Full Control.
Shares pointing at sensitive folders or the root of a drive.
false_positives: Software that creates its own shares.

detect: Collect event 5142 from all machines.
Alert on share changes on workstations (they rarely need shares).
Alert when share permissions grant Everyone or Authenticated Users full control.
Alert when the actor is not a file-server administrator.
investigate: Check what folder the share exposes and who accessed it (5140, 5145).
Build a timeline of what the same account and machine did 30 minutes before and after the event.
Check whether the account or machine also appears in other alerts.
respond: Remove or restrict the share.
Investigate the actor's session.
Preserve the relevant logs before making changes.
prevent: Block inbound SMB between workstations with host firewall rules.
Review at least quarterly who holds the rights involved in this event.
After every incident, feed the lessons learned back into this detection.

pseudocode: FOR EACH event IN Security WHERE EventID == 5142
score = 0
IF is_workstation(event.Computer): score += 2
IF grants_everyone_full(event.NewSD): score += 2
IF event.SubjectUserName NOT IN fileserver_admins: score += 1
IF score >= 2: ALERT Medium "A network share object was added on " + event.Computer

events.attack_context: Many remote administration and lateral movement methods use RPC. Recording RPC attempts can help reconstruct remote actions against a machine, although the volume is high.

key_fields.why: The process handling the RPC call.

watch_for: RPC calls to sensitive interfaces from unexpected machines.

attacks.name: Unusual RPC activity
attacks.summary: Many remote administration and lateral movement methods use RPC. Recording RPC attempts can help reconstruct remote actions against a machine, although the volume is high.
indicators: RPC calls to sensitive interfaces from unexpected machines.
false_positives: Management tools and domain services use RPC constantly.

detect: Collect event 5712 only on key servers (volume is high).
Focus on remote-management interfaces called from workstations.
Send event 5712 to your SIEM and keep at least 90 days of history for investigations.
investigate: Correlate with network logons (4624 type 3) from the same source.
Build a timeline of what the same account and machine did 30 minutes before and after the event.
Check whether the account or machine also appears in other alerts.
respond: Contain the source if the activity is unauthorized.
Preserve the relevant logs before making changes.
If the activity is malicious, open an incident and follow your response playbook.
prevent: Restrict remote management to admin hosts with firewall rules.
Review at least quarterly who holds the rights involved in this event.
After every incident, feed the lessons learned back into this detection.

events.attack_context: Plugging in USB drives or other devices can be used to steal data or introduce malicious hardware. Device events show what was connected, and whether policy allowed or blocked it.

indicators: USB storage on servers or on machines where it is banned.

detect: Collect event 6416 from all machines.
Alert on USB storage on servers or where policy bans it.

Look for file copies to removable drives around that time.

IF event.ClassName == "DiskDrive" AND (is_server(event.Computer) OR usb_banned(event.Computer)):

ELSE IF event.ClassName IN ("Keyboard", "Net") AND is_sensitive(event.Computer):
ALERT Medium "New input/network device on sensitive host"

events.attack_context: Trusts connect domains and forests. An attacker with high privileges might add or change a trust to keep a backdoor into the environment or to link in a domain they control.

attacks.name: Domain trust change
attacks.summary: Trusts connect domains and forests. An attacker with high privileges might add or change a trust to keep a backdoor into the environment or to link in a domain they control.
indicators: Any trust created, changed or removed without an approved change request.

detect: Collect event 4706 from domain controllers.
Alert on every trust change; they should be rare and planned.

investigate: Confirm the change against a change request.

respond: Remove or restore the trust configuration.

prevent: Limit trust management to Enterprise Admins and protect those accounts.

how_to_enable: Open Group Policy Management and edit a GPO linked to the computers you want to monitor.

attacks.name: Audit settings tampering
attacks.summary: Audit settings decide what gets logged. Attackers may narrow auditing on specific files or users, or change how audit failures are handled, so their later actions leave no trace.
indicators: Auditing removed from sensitive files, keys or AD objects.
Per-user audit exclusions for specific accounts.
Security event sources registered by unknown software.
false_positives: Software registering event sources on install.

detect: Collect event 4904 from all machines.
Alert when auditing is removed or reduced on sensitive objects or users.
Alert when the actor is not a security administrator.
investigate: Compare old and new audit settings.
Look for activity on the affected object after the change.
Build a timeline of what the same account and machine did 30 minutes before and after the event.
respond: Restore auditing and review what happened while it was reduced.
Preserve the relevant logs before making changes.
If the activity is malicious, open an incident and follow your response playbook.
prevent: Enforce audit settings through Group Policy.
Limit the 'Manage auditing and security log' right.
Review at least quarterly who holds the rights involved in this event.

ALERT High "An attempt was made to register a security event source on " + event.Computer + " by " + event.SubjectUserName

events.name: A directory service object was created
events.description: A directory service object was created.
how_to_enable: Open Group Policy Management and edit a GPO linked to the computers you want to monitor.
Go to Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Advanced Audit Policy Configuration > DS Access.

events.attack_context: Creating, moving, restoring or deleting Active Directory objects changes who and what exists in the domain. Attackers may create objects for persistence, restore deleted privileged accounts, or delete objects to disrupt operations.
mitre: T1484 Domain or Tenant Policy Modification

key_fields.why: Type of object (user, group, computer, GPO...).

watch_for: Objects created or restored in privileged containers.
Deletion of many objects in a short time.
Changes by accounts that do not administer AD.

attacks.name: Unexpected Active Directory object change
attacks.summary: Creating, moving, restoring or deleting Active Directory objects changes who and what exists in the domain. Attackers may create objects for persistence, restore deleted privileged accounts, or delete objects to disrupt operations.
indicators: Objects created or restored in privileged containers.
Deletion of many objects in a short time.
Changes by accounts that do not administer AD.

detect: Collect event 5137 from domain controllers.
Alert when objects are created, restored or moved in privileged containers.
Alert on mass deletions (many objects in a few minutes).
Alert when the actor is not an AD administrator.
investigate: Identify the actor and source machine.
Review related 5136 attribute changes.
Build a timeline of what the same account and machine did 30 minutes before and after the event.
respond: Restore or remove objects as needed (AD Recycle Bin).
Preserve the relevant logs before making changes.
If the activity is malicious, open an incident and follow your response playbook.
prevent: Enable the AD Recycle Bin.
Delegate AD rights narrowly.
Review at least quarterly who holds the rights involved in this event.

pseudocode: FOR EACH event IN Security WHERE EventID == 5137
IF path_in(event.ObjectDN, privileged_containers): ALERT High "A directory service object was created: " + event.ObjectDN
FOR EACH user IN GROUP Security WHERE EventID == 5141 BY SubjectUserName OVER 10 minutes
IF COUNT(events) >= 50: ALERT High "Mass AD deletion by " + user

events.name: An Active Directory replica source naming context was established
events.description: An Active Directory replica source naming context was established.
how_to_enable: Open Group Policy Management and edit a GPO linked to the computers you want to monitor.
Go to Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Advanced Audit Policy Configuration > DS Access.
Enable 'Audit Directory Service Replication' for Success and/or Failure as needed.
Run 'gpupdate /force' on a test machine and confirm with 'auditpol /get /subcategory:"Directory Service Replication"'.
Forward the Security log to your SIEM (Windows Event Forwarding or an agent).
events.attack_context: Replication keeps domain controllers in sync. Attackers may abuse replication to pull password data or to push their own changes into the directory while pretending to be a domain controller. Replication between machines that are not real DCs is a major red flag.

key_fields.why: The machines replicating; both should be known domain controllers.
Which part of the directory replicated.

watch_for: Replication partners that are not in your list of domain controllers.
New replica sources established outside DC builds.
Long-running replication failures, which can hide changes.

attacks.name: Replication with unknown partner
attacks.summary: Replication keeps domain controllers in sync. Attackers may abuse replication to pull password data or to push their own changes into the directory while pretending to be a domain controller. Replication between machines that are not real DCs is a major red flag.
indicators: Replication partners that are not in your list of domain controllers.
New replica sources established outside DC builds.
Long-running replication failures, which can hide changes.

detect: Collect event 4928 from domain controllers.
Keep an up-to-date list of domain controllers.
Alert when a replication partner is not on the list.
Alert on replication failures lasting more than a few hours.
investigate: Identify the unknown machine and who controls it.
Look for DCSync-style access (4662).

events.name: Certificate Services received a certificate request
events.description: Certificate Services received a certificate request.
how_to_enable: Open Group Policy Management and edit a GPO linked to the computers you want to monitor.
Go to Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Advanced Audit Policy Configuration > Object Access.
Enable 'Audit Certification Services' for Success and/or Failure as needed.
Run 'gpupdate /force' on a test machine and confirm with 'auditpol /get /subcategory:"Certification Services"'.
Forward the Security log to your SIEM (Windows Event Forwarding or an agent).
Also enable auditing in the Certification Authority console (CA properties > Auditing) or with 'certutil -setreg CA\AuditFilter 127', then restart the CA service.
events.attack_context: Certificates can be used to log on as a user. If certificate templates or the CA are misconfigured, attackers may obtain certificates for privileged accounts and use them as long-lasting credentials that survive password resets.
mitre: T1649 Steal or Forge Authentication Certificates

key_fields.why: Links the request, approval and issuance events together.
Account that asked for the certificate.
Who the certificate is for; a different name than the requester deserves review.
Which template was used; some templates allow authentication as any user.

watch_for: Certificates issued where the subject or SAN names a different (especially privileged) user than the requester.
Requests for authentication-capable templates by unusual accounts.
Many requests from one account in a short time.

attacks.name: Certificate services misuse
attacks.summary: Certificates can be used to log on as a user. If certificate templates or the CA are misconfigured, attackers may obtain certificates for privileged accounts and use them as long-lasting credentials that survive password resets.
indicators: Certificates issued where the subject or SAN names a different (especially privileged) user than the requester.
Requests for authentication-capable templates by unusual accounts.
Many requests from one account in a short time.

detect: Enable CA auditing and collect event 4886 from every certificate authority.
For issuance events, alert when the subject or SAN names a different user than the requester.
Alert on template, permission or CA configuration changes outside PKI change windows.
Alert on CA backup, key retrieval or database row deletion by unexpected accounts.
investigate: Identify the requester and template.
Check whether the certificate was used to log on (4768 with certificate details).
Build a timeline of what the same account and machine did 30 minutes before and after the event.
respond: Revoke suspicious certificates and publish a new CRL.
Reverse template or permission changes.
Preserve the relevant logs before making changes.
prevent: Review certificate templates for risky settings.
Require manager approval for sensitive templates.
Review at least quarterly who holds the rights involved in this event.

pseudocode: FOR EACH event IN Security WHERE EventID == 4886
IF event.EventID == 4887 AND subject_user(event) != event.Requester:
ALERT High "Certificate issued for a different user than requester"
ELSE IF event.SubjectUserName NOT IN pki_admins:
ALERT Medium "Certificate Services received a certificate request by " + event.SubjectUserName

how_to_enable: Open Group Policy Management and edit a GPO linked to the computers you want to monitor.
Go to Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Advanced Audit Policy Configuration > Object Access.
Enable 'Audit Certification Services' for Success and/or Failure as needed.
Run 'gpupdate /force' on a test machine and confirm with 'auditpol /get /subcategory:"Certification Services"'.
Forward the Security log to your SIEM (Windows Event Forwarding or an agent).
Also enable auditing in the Certification Authority console (CA properties > Auditing) or with 'certutil -setreg CA\AuditFilter 127', then restart the CA service.
events.attack_context: Operations on the CA itself (starting, stopping, backup, restore, revocation, database changes) matter because a stolen CA backup or key lets an attacker create trusted certificates, and stopping revocation publishing can keep stolen certificates working.
mitre: T1649 Steal or Forge Authentication Certificates
watch_for: CA backups not performed by your backup process (the backup can include the CA key).
The CA service stopped or shut down unexpectedly.
Rows deleted from the certificate database or certificates imported directly.

attacks.name: Certificate services misuse
attacks.summary: Operations on the CA itself (starting, stopping, backup, restore, revocation, database changes) matter because a stolen CA backup or key lets an attacker create trusted certificates, and stopping revocation publishing can keep stolen certificates working.
indicators: CA backups not performed by your backup process (the backup can include the CA key).
The CA service stopped or shut down unexpectedly.
Rows deleted from the certificate database or certificates imported directly.

detect: Enable CA auditing and collect event 4879 from every certificate authority.
For issuance events, alert when the subject or SAN names a different user than the requester.
Alert on template, permission or CA configuration changes outside PKI change windows.
Alert on CA backup, key retrieval or database row deletion by unexpected accounts.
investigate: Identify the requester and template.
Check whether the certificate was used to log on (4768 with certificate details).
Build a timeline of what the same account and machine did 30 minutes before and after the event.
respond: Revoke suspicious certificates and publish a new CRL.
Reverse template or permission changes.
Preserve the relevant logs before making changes.
prevent: Review certificate templates for risky settings.
Require manager approval for sensitive templates.
Review at least quarterly who holds the rights involved in this event.

pseudocode: FOR EACH event IN Security WHERE EventID == 4879
IF event.EventID == 4887 AND subject_user(event) != event.Requester:
ALERT High "Certificate issued for a different user than requester"
ELSE IF event.SubjectUserName NOT IN pki_admins:
ALERT Medium "Certificate Services restore completed by " + event.SubjectUserName

Security settings changed on the responder.

attacks.name: Certificate services misuse
attacks.summary: The OCSP responder tells clients whether a certificate has been revoked. If it is stopped or misconfigured, revoked (for example stolen) certificates may still be accepted.
indicators: The responder stopped outside maintenance.
Security settings changed on the responder.

detect: Enable CA auditing and collect event 5124 from every certificate authority.
For issuance events, alert when the subject or SAN names a different user than the requester.
Alert on template, permission or CA configuration changes outside PKI change windows.
Alert on CA backup, key retrieval or database row deletion by unexpected accounts.
investigate: Identify the requester and template.
Check whether the certificate was used to log on (4768 with certificate details).
Build a timeline of what the same account and machine did 30 minutes before and after the event.
respond: Revoke suspicious certificates and publish a new CRL.
Reverse template or permission changes.
Preserve the relevant logs before making changes.
prevent: Review certificate templates for risky settings.
Require manager approval for sensitive templates.
Review at least quarterly who holds the rights involved in this event.

pseudocode: FOR EACH event IN Security WHERE EventID == 5124
IF event.EventID == 4887 AND subject_user(event) != event.Requester:
ALERT High "Certificate issued for a different user than requester"
ELSE IF event.SubjectUserName NOT IN pki_admins:
ALERT Medium "A security setting was updated on OCSP Responder Service by " + event.SubjectUserName

events.name: A request was submitted to OCSP Responder Service
events.description: A request was submitted to the OCSP Responder service.
how_to_enable: Open Group Policy Management and edit a GPO linked to the computers you want to monitor.
Go to Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Advanced Audit Policy Configuration > Object Access.
Enable 'Audit Certification Services' for Success and/or Failure as needed.
Run 'gpupdate /force' on a test machine and confirm with 'auditpol /get /subcategory:"Certification Services"'.
Forward the Security log to your SIEM (Windows Event Forwarding or an agent).

events.attack_context: Key and cryptographic operation events show use of stored private keys. Attackers who reach a machine may try to export or use private keys (for example certificate or machine keys) to impersonate it. These events are very noisy, so they are mostly useful during investigations.
mitre: T1649 Steal or Forge Authentication Certificates

key_fields.why: Which key and what was done with it.

watch_for: Private key export or access by unfamiliar processes.
Crypto self-test or primitive failures on servers (possible tampering or faulty hardware).

attacks.name: Unusual private key activity
attacks.summary: Key and cryptographic operation events show use of stored private keys. Attackers who reach a machine may try to export or use private keys (for example certificate or machine keys) to impersonate it. These events are very noisy, so they are mostly useful during investigations.
indicators: Private key export or access by unfamiliar processes.
Crypto self-test or primitive failures on servers (possible tampering or faulty hardware).
false_positives: Normal TLS, certificate and key operations (very high volume).

detect: Collect event 5056 only on key servers (volume is high).
Focus on export operations and on keys belonging to certificates that allow authentication.
Alert on crypto self-test or primitive failures on servers.
investigate: Identify the process and account using the key.
Build a timeline of what the same account and machine did 30 minutes before and after the event.
Check whether the account or machine also appears in other alerts.
respond: Replace (re-key) certificates whose private keys may have been exposed.
Preserve the relevant logs before making changes.
If the activity is malicious, open an incident and follow your response playbook.
prevent: Mark private keys as non-exportable.
Store high-value keys in a TPM or HSM.
Review at least quarterly who holds the rights involved in this event.

pseudocode: FOR EACH event IN Security WHERE EventID == 5056
IF event.Operation CONTAINS "Export" AND basename(event.ProcessName) NOT IN key_tools:
ALERT High "Private key export by " + event.ProcessName
ELSE IF event.EventID IN (5057, 5060) AND is_server(event.Computer):
ALERT Medium "Cryptographic failure on " + event.Computer

indicators: Private key export or access by unfamiliar processes.
Crypto self-test or primitive failures on servers (possible tampering or faulty hardware).
false_positives: Normal TLS, certificate and key operations (very high volume).

detect: Collect event 5064 only on key servers (volume is high).
Focus on export operations and on keys belonging to certificates that allow authentication.
Alert on crypto self-test or primitive failures on servers.
investigate: Identify the process and account using the key.
Build a timeline of what the same account and machine did 30 minutes before and after the event.
Check whether the account or machine also appears in other alerts.
respond: Replace (re-key) certificates whose private keys may have been exposed.
Preserve the relevant logs before making changes.
If the activity is malicious, open an incident and follow your response playbook.
prevent: Mark private keys as non-exportable.
Store high-value keys in a TPM or HSM.
Review at least quarterly who holds the rights involved in this event.

pseudocode: FOR EACH event IN Security WHERE EventID == 5064
IF event.Operation CONTAINS "Export" AND basename(event.ProcessName) NOT IN key_tools:
ALERT High "Private key export by " + event.ProcessName
ELSE IF event.EventID IN (5057, 5060) AND is_server(event.Computer):
ALERT Medium "Cryptographic failure on " + event.Computer

events.name: A cryptographic context modification was attempted
events.description: A change was attempted to a cryptographic context.
how_to_enable: Open Group Policy Management and edit a GPO linked to the computers you want to monitor.
Go to Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Advanced Audit Policy Configuration > System.
Enable 'Audit Other System Events' for Success and/or Failure as needed.
Run 'gpupdate /force' on a test machine and confirm with 'auditpol /get /subcategory:"Other System Events"'.
Forward the Security log to your SIEM (Windows Event Forwarding or an agent).

events.name: The following policy was active when the Windows Firewall started
events.description: Lists the firewall policy that was active when the Windows Firewall started.
how_to_enable: Open Group Policy Management and edit a GPO linked to the computers you want to monitor.
Go to Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Advanced Audit Policy Configuration > Policy Change.
Enable 'Audit MPSSVC Rule-Level Policy Change' for Success and/or Failure as needed.
Run 'gpupdate /force' on a test machine and confirm with 'auditpol /get /subcategory:"MPSSVC Rule-Level Policy Change"'.
Forward the Security log to your SIEM (Windows Event Forwarding or an agent).
events.attack_context: Attackers often add or loosen firewall rules so their tools can accept inbound connections, reach command-and-control servers, or allow remote access such as Remote Desktop. Resetting or switching profiles can quietly remove protective rules.
mitre: T1562.004 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify System Firewall

key_fields.why: What the rule allows or blocks.
Who or what made the change.
Domain, Private or Public network profile.

watch_for: New allow rules for programs in user-writable folders.
Rules opening remote access ports (3389, 5985/5986, 445) to any address.
Changes made by scripts or command-line tools rather than Group Policy.
Firewall reset to defaults or turned off for a profile.

attacks.name: Firewall rule tampering
attacks.summary: Attackers often add or loosen firewall rules so their tools can accept inbound connections, reach command-and-control servers, or allow remote access such as Remote Desktop. Resetting or switching profiles can quietly remove protective rules.
indicators: New allow rules for programs in user-writable folders.
Rules opening remote access ports (3389, 5985/5986, 445) to any address.
Changes made by scripts or command-line tools rather than Group Policy.
Firewall reset to defaults or turned off for a profile.
false_positives: Software installers adding their own rules.

detect: Collect event 4944 from all machines.
Ignore changes applied by Group Policy.
Alert on local changes that allow inbound remote-access ports to any address.
Alert on rules for programs in user-writable folders, or firewall resets and profile disables.
investigate: Identify the modifying program and account.
Check whether the new rule has been used (5156).
Build a timeline of what the same account and machine did 30 minutes before and after the event.
respond: Remove the rule or restore the firewall policy.
Isolate the machine if a malicious program added it.
Preserve the relevant logs before making changes.
prevent: Enforce firewall policy with Group Policy and block local rule merging on sensitive machines.
Review at least quarterly who holds the rights involved in this event.
After every incident, feed the lessons learned back into this detection.

pseudocode: FOR EACH event IN Security WHERE EventID == 4944
IF event.ModifyingApplication ENDS WITH "svchost.exe" AND gpo_update_near(event): CONTINUE
risky = event.Action == "Allow" AND event.Direction == "Inbound"
IF risky OR references_user_writable_path(event.ApplicationPath) OR event.EventID IN (4949, 4950):
ALERT High "The following policy was active when the Windows Firewall started on " + event.Computer

watch_for: New allow rules for programs in user-writable folders.

Changes made by scripts or command-line tools rather than Group Policy.
Firewall reset to defaults or turned off for a profile.

attacks.name: Firewall rule tampering
attacks.summary: Attackers often add or loosen firewall rules so their tools can accept inbound connections, reach command-and-control servers, or allow remote access such as Remote Desktop. Resetting or switching profiles can quietly remove protective rules.
indicators: New allow rules for programs in user-writable folders.
Rules opening remote access ports (3389, 5985/5986, 445) to any address.
Changes made by scripts or command-line tools rather than Group Policy.
Firewall reset to defaults or turned off for a profile.
false_positives: Software installers adding their own rules.

detect: Collect event 4958 from all machines.
Ignore changes applied by Group Policy.
Alert on local changes that allow inbound remote-access ports to any address.
Alert on rules for programs in user-writable folders, or firewall resets and profile disables.
investigate: Identify the modifying program and account.
Check whether the new rule has been used (5156).
Build a timeline of what the same account and machine did 30 minutes before and after the event.
respond: Remove the rule or restore the firewall policy.
Isolate the machine if a malicious program added it.
Preserve the relevant logs before making changes.
prevent: Enforce firewall policy with Group Policy and block local rule merging on sensitive machines.
Review at least quarterly who holds the rights involved in this event.
After every incident, feed the lessons learned back into this detection.

how_to_enable: Open Group Policy Management and edit a GPO linked to the computers you want to monitor.
Go to Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Advanced Audit Policy Configuration > Object Access.
Enable 'Audit Filtering Platform Packet Drop' for Success and/or Failure as needed.
Run 'gpupdate /force' on a test machine and confirm with 'auditpol /get /subcategory:"Filtering Platform Packet Drop"'.
Forward the Security log to your SIEM (Windows Event Forwarding or an agent).
events.attack_context: Dropped packets can reveal network scanning (many blocked attempts across ports) or flooding against a machine. On their own they are usually noise.

key_fields.why: Program that made or received the connection.
Inbound or outbound, TCP or UDP.

watch_for: One source hitting many ports or many machines (scanning).
WFP entering DoS defensive mode (5148).

attacks.name: Network scanning or flooding
attacks.summary: Dropped packets can reveal network scanning (many blocked attempts across ports) or flooding against a machine. On their own they are usually noise.
indicators: One source hitting many ports or many machines (scanning).
WFP entering DoS defensive mode (5148).

detect: Collect event 5146 on selected servers.
Group dropped packets by source address.
Alert when one source hits many ports or many machines in a short time.
Alert immediately on DoS defensive mode (5148).
investigate: Identify the source machine and what is running on it.
Build a timeline of what the same account and machine did 30 minutes before and after the event.
Check whether the account or machine also appears in other alerts.
respond: Block or contain the source.
Preserve the relevant logs before making changes.
If the activity is malicious, open an incident and follow your response playbook.
prevent: Segment the network and limit which machines can reach servers.
Review at least quarterly who holds the rights involved in this event.
After every incident, feed the lessons learned back into this detection.

pseudocode: FOR EACH src IN GROUP Security WHERE EventID == 5146 BY SourceAddress OVER 10 minutes
IF src IN scanner_allow_list: CONTINUE
IF COUNT DISTINCT DestPort >= 50 OR COUNT DISTINCT DestAddress >= 20:
ALERT Medium "Possible scan from " + src

events.name: The following callout was present when the Windows Filtering Platform Base Filtering Engine started
events.description: Lists a WFP callout present when the Base Filtering Engine started.
how_to_enable: Open Group Policy Management and edit a GPO linked to the computers you want to monitor.
Go to Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Advanced Audit Policy Configuration > Policy Change.
Enable 'Audit Filtering Platform Policy Change' for Success and/or Failure as needed.
Run 'gpupdate /force' on a test machine and confirm with 'auditpol /get /subcategory:"Filtering Platform Policy Change"'.
Forward the Security log to your SIEM (Windows Event Forwarding or an agent).
events.attack_context: WFP filters and callouts are what firewalls and many security products use to inspect traffic. Unexpected changes can mean something is adding its own filtering or weakening existing filters.
mitre: T1562.004 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify System Firewall
watch_for: WFP objects changed by unknown processes.
Filters that block traffic from security or monitoring software.

attacks.name: Filtering platform change
attacks.summary: WFP filters and callouts are what firewalls and many security products use to inspect traffic. Unexpected changes can mean something is adding its own filtering or weakening existing filters.
indicators: WFP objects changed by unknown processes.
Filters that block traffic from security or monitoring software.

detect: Collect event 5440 from servers.
Treat startup listings as inventory; compare them with a baseline.
Alert on changes by processes that are not known security products.
investigate: Identify the process that changed WFP objects.
Build a timeline of what the same account and machine did 30 minutes before and after the event.
Check whether the account or machine also appears in other alerts.
respond: Remove unknown filters and isolate the machine if needed.
Preserve the relevant logs before making changes.
If the activity is malicious, open an incident and follow your response playbook.
prevent: Restrict administrator rights.
Review at least quarterly who holds the rights involved in this event.
After every incident, feed the lessons learned back into this detection.

pseudocode: FOR EACH event IN Security WHERE EventID == 5440
IF event.EventID BETWEEN 5440 AND 5444:
IF event.ObjectName NOT IN wfp_baseline: ALERT Low "New WFP object at startup"
ELSE IF process_name(event.ProcessId) NOT IN security_products:
ALERT Medium "The following callout was present when the Windows Filtering Platform Base Filtering Engine started by unknown process"

Enable 'Audit IPsec Main Mode' for Success and/or Failure as needed.
Run 'gpupdate /force' on a test machine and confirm with 'auditpol /get /subcategory:"IPsec Main Mode"'.
Forward the Security log to your SIEM (Windows Event Forwarding or an agent).

detect: Collect event 4980 on machines that use IPsec.

investigate: Identify the remote machine and check its configuration and certificates.

Alert on integrity, replay or clear-text drops (possible tampering).
investigate: Identify the remote machine and check its configuration and certificates.
Build a timeline of what the same account and machine did 30 minutes before and after the event.
Check whether the account or machine also appears in other alerts.
respond: Block the remote address if it is not a known peer.
Preserve the relevant logs before making changes.
If the activity is malicious, open an incident and follow your response playbook.
prevent: Use certificate or Kerberos authentication rather than pre-shared keys.
Review at least quarterly who holds the rights involved in this event.
After every incident, feed the lessons learned back into this detection.

pseudocode: FOR EACH remote IN GROUP Security WHERE EventID == 4965 BY RemoteAddress OVER 30 minutes
IF COUNT(events) >= 20 AND remote NOT IN ipsec_peers:

events.name: IPsec Services was started
events.description: IPsec Services was started.
how_to_enable: Open Group Policy Management and edit a GPO linked to the computers you want to monitor.
Go to Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Advanced Audit Policy Configuration > System.
Enable 'Audit IPsec Driver' for Success and/or Failure as needed.

Forward the Security log to your SIEM (Windows Event Forwarding or an agent).

events.attack_context: IPsec policy decides which traffic must be protected. Changing or deleting rules and crypto sets can weaken that protection, so unexpected changes on important servers deserve a check.

key_fields.why: Who or what made the change.

watch_for: Connection security rules deleted or weakened outside Group Policy.

Enable 'Audit Filtering Platform Policy Change' for Success and/or Failure as needed.
Run 'gpupdate /force' on a test machine and confirm with 'auditpol /get /subcategory:"Filtering Platform Policy Change"'.
Forward the Security log to your SIEM (Windows Event Forwarding or an agent).
events.attack_context: IPsec policy decides which traffic must be protected. Changing or deleting rules and crypto sets can weaken that protection, so unexpected changes on important servers deserve a check.

key_fields.why: Who or what made the change.

watch_for: Connection security rules deleted or weakened outside Group Policy.
Failures to apply IPsec policy (machines left without it).

attacks.name: IPsec policy change or failure
attacks.summary: IPsec policy decides which traffic must be protected. Changing or deleting rules and crypto sets can weaken that protection, so unexpected changes on important servers deserve a check.
indicators: Connection security rules deleted or weakened outside Group Policy.
Failures to apply IPsec policy (machines left without it).

detect: Collect event 5044 on machines that use IPsec.
Alert on deleted or modified rules outside Group Policy.
Alert when policy fails to apply repeatedly.
investigate: Compare the active IPsec policy with the expected one.
Build a timeline of what the same account and machine did 30 minutes before and after the event.
Check whether the account or machine also appears in other alerts.
respond: Restore the IPsec policy.
Preserve the relevant logs before making changes.
If the activity is malicious, open an incident and follow your response playbook.
prevent: Manage IPsec policy only through Group Policy.
Review at least quarterly who holds the rights involved in this event.
After every incident, feed the lessons learned back into this detection.

key_fields.why: User who tried to connect (VPN, Wi-Fi, 802.1X).
Client device identifier (e.g. MAC or phone number).
The VPN server, access point or switch that forwarded the request.
Why access was denied or discarded.

watch_for: Many denials for one account or from one device.
Successful VPN access from unusual locations or devices.
NPS account lockouts (6279).

indicators: Many denials for one account or from one device.

NPS account lockouts (6279).

detect: Collect event 6272 from all Network Policy Servers.

Alert on successful access from devices never seen before for privileged accounts.
investigate: Check the user's recent sign-ins and locations.
Identify the device from CallingStationID.

respond: Disable the account or device if compromised.
Reset credentials.
Preserve the relevant logs before making changes.
prevent: Require MFA or certificate authentication for VPN and Wi-Fi.
